procedural_history.impugned_order: Order passed by the Chief of the Army Staff, after setting aside the order passed by Maj-Gen. Hira, which revoked the earlier sentence and sentenced him to be cashiered and to suffer rigorous imprisonment for two years. The said sentence was duly confirmed by the Chief of the Army Staff.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution, seeking to quash the order passed by the Chief of the Army Staff. The Supreme Court considered whether any fundamental right of the petitioner had been violated, specifically Article 21, and found that the procedure established by law had been completely followed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the confirmation of a court-martial's sentence must be by the specific officer who convened the court, or if it can be done by a successor in the same post or a superior authority.

facts: The court-martial was convened by a Major-General.
The officer who later directed a revision of the sentence was a Brigadier who was officiating in the same post as the Major-General (Officer Commanding the 23rd Mountain Division).
The final confirmation of the sentence was done by the Chief of Army Staff, an authority superior to the convening officer.
law: Section 157 of the Army Act states that the findings and sentences of summary general courts-martial may be confirmed by the 'convening officer or if he so directs, by an authority superior to him'.
The Court referenced Section 112 of the Army Act to show that the terms 'officer' and 'authority' are used interchangeably and refer to the same person holding a post.

The Court drew a comparison to decisions under Article 311 of the Constitution, where disciplinary power can be exercised by the authority currently competent to appoint an officer, not necessarily the original appointing authority.
application: The Court rejected the petitioner's argument that there was a meaningful distinction between the terms 'convening officer' and 'authority'. It held that the words refer to the post, not the specific individual holding it at a given time.

The Court reasoned that accepting the petitioner's argument would lead to impractical consequences, as the entire procedure would have to be redone if the original convening officer was transferred, retired, or died.
The Court found that since the Brigadier who directed the revision held the same command post as the Major-General who convened the court, his action was valid. The power is attached to the office.
Furthermore, the final confirmation was by the Chief of Army Staff, who was an 'authority superior to' the convening officer, a procedure explicitly permitted by Section 157.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's contention, holding that the confirmation of a court-martial's sentence is not limited to the specific individual who convened the court. The power is vested in the office, and therefore, it can be validly exercised by a successor in the same post or by a superior authority as permitted by the Army Act.

issue.issue_text: Whether an accused must be given an opportunity to be heard before the confirming authority orders the court-martial to reconsider and revise the sentence, especially when it leads to an enhancement.

facts: A Court-Martial found the petitioner guilty and sentenced him 'to be cashiered'.
The Confirming Officer, believing the sentence was not commensurate with the gravity of the offense, sent the case back to the Court-Martial for reconsideration and potential upward revision.
When the Court-Martial reassembled to revise the sentence, the petitioner was informed of the Confirming Officer's reasons and was asked if he wanted to address the court.
The petitioner declined the opportunity to address the Court-Martial during the revision hearing.
The Court-Martial then enhanced the sentence.
law: The Army Act (Section 160) explicitly allows a confirming authority to order a sentence to be revised once.
The procedures laid down in the Code of Criminal Procedure do not automatically apply to court-martial proceedings.
The principles of natural justice do not require a hearing at every stage of a proceeding.
application: The Court determined that a hearing before the confirming authority was not a requirement under the Army Act or the principles of natural justice in this context.
The Court emphasized that the petitioner had already been given a full opportunity to present his case before the Court-Martial during the initial trial.

Crucially, the petitioner was given a second opportunity to be heard directly by the Court-Martial when it was reconsidering the sentence. He was made aware of the confirming authority's reasoning and could have argued against it at that time.
By failing to avail himself of the opportunity to address the Court-Martial during the revision, the petitioner could not later complain that he was not heard by the confirming authority.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that there was no violation of natural justice. The petitioner's right to be heard was satisfied by the opportunity given to him to address the Court-Martial during the revision process itself. Therefore, a separate hearing before the confirming authority prior to it ordering the revision was not necessary.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, under Article 32, can examine the sufficiency or correctness of the evidence considered by a court-martial.

facts: The petitioner urged that the confirming authority for his court-martial proceeded on an incorrect basis regarding the evidence available against him.
law: Under Article 136(2) of the Constitution, the Supreme Court is barred from granting special leave to appeal any judgment, determination, or order from a court or tribunal constituted under any law relating to the Armed Forces.
application: The Court stated explicitly that in a petition filed under Article 32, it "cannot go into the evidence in support of the charge against the petitioner."

The Court referenced the constitutional prohibition in Article 136(2) to support its position. Although the current case was under Article 32 (writ jurisdiction) and not Article 136 (special leave to appeal), the Court used this provision to illustrate the clear constitutional intent to limit its role as an appellate body over military tribunals.

Therefore, the Court's function is not to re-weigh or assess the sufficiency and correctness of the evidence, which is a task for an appellate court, a role the Constitution explicitly denies it in military matters.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that it cannot examine the sufficiency or correctness of the evidence considered by a court-martial when hearing a petition under Article 32, citing a direct prohibition on such an inquiry and the broader constitutional principle of limited judicial review over armed forces tribunals.

issue.issue_text: Whether the order directing revision of the sentence was framed in such a manner that it left the court-martial with no alternative but to enhance the sentence, thereby violating principles of natural justice.

facts: An army officer was found guilty of robbery by a Court-Martial and sentenced 'to be cashiered'.
The confirming authority, Maj-Gen. Hira, found this sentence to be 'wholly inadequate' given the gravity of the offense (robbery committed while serving as a liberating force in Bangladesh).
He sent the sentence back to the Court-Martial for revision, providing strong reasons for his opinion.
The Court-Martial, after reconsidering, enhanced the sentence to cashiering plus two years of rigorous imprisonment.
The petitioner argued that the confirming authority's order was so strongly worded that it compelled the Court-Martial and left it with no alternative but to enhance the sentence.
law: Under Section 160 of the Army Act, a confirming authority may order a sentence to be revised once.
Under Section 158 of the Army Act, a confirming authority has the power to mitigate, remit, or commute a punishment to a lesser one.
The power to direct a revision can only be exercised once. If the court-martial reaffirms its original sentence after revision, the confirming authority cannot order another revision.
application: The Court reasoned that since a confirming authority can already reduce a sentence on their own (under Section 158), an order to revise a sentence (under Section 160) necessarily implies that the authority considers the punishment too lenient and believes it should be revised upwards.

The Court found that providing strong reasons for this view was not a form of compulsion, but rather a lawful and transparent exercise of the authority's power. It was deemed better than a bald, unexplained directive.

The Court pointed to specific language in the revision order which showed the Court-Martial was not being compelled. The order stated it was 'in no way intending [to dictate] the quantum of punishment' and referred to what should happen 'should the court martial decide to enhance the sentence,' implying the decision was still theirs to make.

Crucially, the Court noted that the confirming authority's power of revision can only be used once. If the Court-Martial had disagreed and reaffirmed its original sentence, the confirming authority would have been powerless to force a change. This demonstrates that the final decision-making power remained with the Court-Martial.
Furthermore, the petitioner was given an opportunity to address the Court-Martial during the revision process and argue against the confirming authority's reasoning, but he declined to do so.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's argument, concluding that the order directing revision did not violate principles of natural justice. The confirming authority acted within its statutory powers, and the Court-Martial was not compelled or left with no alternative; it retained the ultimate freedom to decide on the sentence, as evidenced by the limits on the revision power and the language of the order itself.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the confirmation of a court-martial's sentence must be by the specific officer who convened the court, or if it can be done by a successor in the same post or a superior authority.
appellant_arguments: Based on Section 157 of the Army Act, there is a distinction between the 'convening officer' and 'an authority superior to him'.
Confirmation can only be done by the specific individual who was the convening officer and no other person.
The officer who directed the revision of the sentence was a Brigadier, while the court was convened by a Major-General, which is improper.
respondent_arguments: The distinction between 'officer' and 'authority' is without substance; they refer to the same person holding the post.
Accepting the appellant's argument would lead to impractical consequences, requiring a new trial if the original convening officer is transferred, retires, or dies.
The principle is similar to Article 311 of the Constitution, where a successor in a post can exercise the powers of that post.
In this case, the confirmation was ultimately done by the Chief of Army Staff, an authority higher in rank than the convening officer, which is permissible.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an accused must be given an opportunity to be heard before the confirming authority orders the court-martial to reconsider and revise the sentence, especially when it leads to an enhancement.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner should have been given a hearing by the confirming authority before an upward revision of the sentence was ordered.
Not providing a hearing before ordering a revision that leads to an enhanced sentence is a violation of the principles of natural justice.
respondent_arguments: There is no requirement under the Army Act or principles of natural justice for the confirming authority to grant a hearing before ordering a revision of the sentence.
Accepting this contention would wrongly imply that all procedures from the Code of Criminal Procedure apply to court-martials, which the Constitution indicates they do not.
The petitioner already had a full opportunity to present his case and contentions before the court-martial.
The petitioner had an available remedy under Section 164 of the Army Act to submit a petition to the final confirming authority (Chief of the Army Staff), but he failed to do so.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, under Article 32, can examine the sufficiency or correctness of the evidence considered by a court-martial.
appellant_arguments: The confirming authority's order for revision was based on an incorrect assessment of the evidence available against the petitioner.
respondent_arguments: The Supreme Court cannot go into the sufficiency or correctness of the evidence in a court-martial proceeding.
Article 136(2) of the Constitution explicitly bars the Court from granting special leave in respect of judgments from tribunals related to the Armed Forces.
Under Article 32, the Court's review is limited to whether a fundamental right has been violated, specifically Article 21, which requires that the procedure established by law has been followed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the order directing revision of the sentence was framed in such a manner that it left the court-martial with no alternative but to enhance the sentence, thereby violating principles of natural justice.
appellant_arguments: The order directing revision was framed in such strong terms that it compelled the court-martial and left it with no alternative but to enhance the sentence.
The revised sentence was not a free act of the court-martial but was forced upon them by the confirming authority's observations, which violates natural justice.
respondent_arguments: The confirming authority has the power to mitigate or remit punishment, so when a revision is ordered, it inherently implies that the authority finds the sentence inadequate and believes it should be revised upwards.
Objecting to the direction for upward revision is tantamount to objecting to the provisions of the Army Act itself (Section 158).
The confirming authority provided reasons for his opinion, which is legally unexceptionable.

The order explicitly stated that the court-martial was not bound by the opinion, using phrases like 'Whilst in no way intending the quantum of punishment to be awarded' and 'should the court martial decide to enhance the sentence', which preserved the court's discretion.

cases.case_name: A. K. Kraipak & Ors. etc. v. Union of India & Ors.
cases.principle: What particular rule of natural justice should apply to a given case depends on its facts and circumstances, the legal framework of the inquiry, and the constitution of the tribunal. The court must decide if observing a rule is necessary for a just decision.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In matters concerning the Armed Forces, the principles of natural justice operate in areas not covered by a validly made law and do not supplant the specific procedure established by that law. Where the procedure established by the Army Act has been fully complied with, the requirements of Article 21 of the Constitution are met. A confirming authority is not required by the principles of natural justice to grant a hearing to an accused before directing a court-martial to revise a sentence, as this power is conferred by the statute itself. The Supreme Court's jurisdiction under Article 32 in such cases is limited to determining if a fundamental right has been violated and does not extend to re-examining the evidence.
obiter: A useful comparison can be made to decisions under Article 311 of the Constitution, where it has been held that the power to deal with an officer can be exercised by an authority lower in rank than the one who originally appointed the officer, if at the relevant time that authority was competent to appoint.
It was open to the petitioner to have availed himself of the remedy provided under Section 164 of the Army Act of presenting a petition to the confirming officer.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court's jurisdiction to review a court-martial's decision under Article 32 is strictly limited to determining whether the procedure established by the relevant law, in this case the Army Act, has been followed. The Court cannot re-examine the sufficiency of evidence, nor can it import principles of natural justice, such as a right to be heard before a sentence revision, that are not provided for in the statute, as the Constitution clearly distinguishes between the procedures for civil cases and those for the Armed Forces.
legal_tests_applied: Article 21 (Procedure Established by Law): The court's review is confined to whether the procedure established by law has been completely followed.
Article 32 (Scope of Review): In petitions under Article 32, the court can only consider whether a fundamental right of the petitioner has been violated.

Article 136(2) (Constitutional Bar): The court is constitutionally barred from granting special leave in respect of any judgment, determination or order passed by any court or tribunal constituted under any law relating to the Armed Forces.

Principles of Natural Justice: The court considered whether rules of natural justice operate in areas not covered by the statute, concluding that what rule applies depends on the framework of the law and that no such rule was violated in this case.
why_appellant_lost: The Supreme Court cannot go into the evidence in support of the charge against the petitioner, as its review under Article 32 is limited to procedural compliance under Article 21, and it is further barred by Article 136(2).

The contention that the petitioner should have been given a hearing before the sentence was revised upwards cannot be accepted, as it is not a requirement under the Army Act or the principles of natural justice in this context.

The order directing revision was not coercive; the confirming authority is entitled under the Army Act to find a sentence inadequate and give reasons for that view, and in this case, the authority explicitly left the discretion regarding the punishment to the court-martial.
The petitioner failed to avail himself of the statutory remedy provided under Section 164 of the Army Act to present a petition to the confirming officer, the Chief of the Army Staff.
why_respondent_won: The procedure established by law as required under Article 21 of the Constitution was completely followed in this case.
The Constitution makes clear indications that the provisions which are applicable to all the civil cases are not applicable to cases of Armed Personnel.

When a sentence is directed to be revised by the confirming authority, it necessarily means that the authority considers the punishment inadequate and should be revised upwards; to object to this is to object to the provisions of section 158 of the Army Act itself.
The confirming authority, instead of baldly stating the sentence was inadequate, gave reasons for his opinion, which is legally unexceptionable and left the final discretion to the court.
policy_considerations: To accept the contention that a hearing must be given before sentence revision would mean that all the procedure laid down by the Code of Criminal Procedure should be adopted in respect of the court martial, a contention which cannot be accepted in the face of the very clear indications in the Constitution that the provisions which are applicable to all the civil cases are not applicable to cases of Armed Personnel.
